title: How to use a floor stand for cross-stitch
subtitle: Setting up and using a freestanding frame holder so both hands are free
excerpt: A floor stand holds the hoop or scroll frame upright without the stitcher holding it, freeing both hands. One hand guides the needle down through the fabric; the other waits below the hoop to pass the needle back up. The stand needs to be adjusted to a height and angle that keeps the fabric at eye level with no neck or shoulder strain.
sourceNotes: Floor stand usage for cross-stitch. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: at a fixed position so both hands are free to work the needle. The needle is passed through the fabric with one hand above the hoop and caught by the other hand below, then returned the same way. This two-handed technique is faster than working one-handed once it is established.
Setting up and using the stand

Position the stand to the side of your chair, not in front. Most floor stands have an arm that extends over the lap; the base sits to one side. Adjust the arm so the fabric hangs at the level of your lap when seated.

Mount the hoop or scroll frame in the stand's clamp. Tighten the clamp enough that the fabric does not shift during stitching. Adjust the tilt angle so the front face of the fabric is facing you comfortably, not angled away.
Sit so your elbows are relaxed at your sides. The stitching position should feel comfortable with no reaching forward. If you are straining to reach the fabric, adjust the arm length or height.

Begin stitching with one hand above the frame and one hand below. Push the needle through a fabric hole with the top hand, pinch the tip from below with the bottom hand, and return it back up through the next hole. This two-handed motion becomes smooth and fast with practice.

Check the stand's stability after the first few minutes. Floor stands can shift on carpet or smooth flooring. Place the base on an anti-slip mat or add weight to it if necessary. The stand should be firm and not rock when you are working.

items.symptom: The stand rocks or tips when stitching
items.cause: The base is too light for the reach of the arm, or the stand is on an uneven surface.
items.fix: Place a heavy book on the base, or use an anti-slip mat. Some floor stands have adjustable base weights. If the stand continues to tip, check that the arm extension is not at maximum length, which increases the lever arm.

items.symptom: The fabric angle keeps shifting mid-session
items.cause: The tilt clamp is not fully tightened, or the vibration of stitching is loosening it.
items.fix: Fully tighten the tilt lock before starting. Some stands have a secondary locking nut; check that it is engaged. If the clamp is worn, a thin rubber washer between the clamp faces improves grip.

content.text: A floor stand is most useful on large projects that take many hours. For a first project, a hoop held in the hand is often easier to manage. Once the two-handed stabbing motion is established, however, stitching with a stand is noticeably faster and reduces hand fatigue.
